chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, who said:

A man from our companions died without making a will, so his case was referred to the judge of Kufa, who appointed 'Abd al-Hamid as the guardian of his estate. The man had left behind minor heirs, female slaves, and movable property. 'Abd al-Hamid sold the movable property, but when he intended to sell the female slaves, his heart weakened regarding their sale because the deceased had not appointed him as his executor by will, and his guardianship was by the order of the judge, as they are 'furuj' (parts/exposed). I mentioned this to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) and said to him: 'A man from our companions dies without appointing anyone as executor and leaves female slaves, so the judge appoints one of us to sell them, or I said: one of us takes charge of that, and his heart weakens because they are furuj. What do you think about that?' He said: 'If the guardian is like you or like 'Abd al-Hamid, there is no harm.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a judge-appointed guardian selling the estate of a deceased person who left no will?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the Shia juristic principle of *al-Qadi al-Qadi* (the judge as guardian) in the absence of a will, specifically addressing the sale of female slaves (*jawari*) as part of the estate's liquidation. The Imam’s response highlights that the validity of the guardian's action depends on his personal reliability (*thiqa*) and competence rather than the source of his appointment, distinguishing between the legal authority of the judge and the moral weight of the guardian's character.
